extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of Rabelais; general readers interested in early-modern divination and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition (in narrative form) of methods for divining the future used by Pantagruel and company: Virgilian lots (opening Virgil and taking a line), dice-based selection, and dream incubation/interpretation, with procedural rules, symbolic interpretations, cautions, and authorities cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virgilian lottery (opening Virgil for answers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a verse from Virgil by opening the book and choosing a line (often via lots or dice) to answer a question about the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure illustrated: open Virgil, pick the nth line corresponding to the cast/result and read that verse as a response. The text gives many historical exempla (e.g., Alexander Severus, Adrian, Claudius, others) where Virgilian lots purportedly foretold important events such as elevation to the empire. The narrator nonetheless warns against accepting infallibility from such results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting dice as illicit/deceitful (condemnation of games of chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel pronounces games of dice (and similar lotteries like cockfighting) deceitful, abusive, illicitous, and scandalous; a social and moral danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit moral/legal condemnation: Gargantua forbade dice throughout his realms, burned the moulds and draughts, and suppressed the practice as a 'most dangerous plague and infection' to the commonwealth. Dice are described as baited hooks of the devil. This is offered both as moral advice and as a reason to distrust dice-based determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-dice Virgil line-selection method (practical procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three dice: throw them, sum the pips, and take the corresponding line/row of the opened page of Virgil as the lot's answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: Panurge throws three dice (casts 5,6,5 summing to 16) and chooses the 16th line. The method is shown in play, with characters debating interpretation and invoking ritual trappings (invoking deities, setting nails to open the page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of an expert interpreter for dreams and lots
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams and mysterious verses require a dexterous, learned, skilled expounder—an oniropolist or interpreter—to read and explain their true meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited (Hippocrates, Plato, Artemidorus, etc.) and the claim that the soul's reports are imperfect without a skilled interpreter. The text explicitly recommends choosing a learned, wise, industrious expounder to interpret somniatory vaticinations rightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for reliable prophetic dreams (incubation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain trustworthy prophetic dreams one must prepare the body and mind: avoid certain foods, moderate eating, avoid passions, and sleep soundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prescriptions: abstain from wine (Amphiaraus recommended three days without wine and 24 hours without food, though Pantagruel moderates this), do not eat hare or other flesh for the pre-sleep meal, avoid beans, polyp (preak), coleworts, cabbage, and 'windy victuals' that disturb the brain. Recommended light fruits (Eusebian/Bergamot pears, one pippin apple, little plums, a few cherries) and pure fountain-water to drink. Emphasis on moderation: over-long fasting is criticized as making spirits dry and writings jejune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state required for divinatory dreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: The dreamer must have a calm, peaceful, untroubled mind—free from human passions (love, hatred, fear, hope)—so the divine part (Nous/Mens) can apprehend future things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Proteus: transformations obscure prophecy; only when restored to natural form can he prophesy. Thus Panurge is told to denude his mind of distracting passions before sleep to receive clear visions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sleep environment and bodily repose (avoid distractions/noises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable dreams require the body to be at rest and free from physical annoyances and external noises which distract the soul's capacity to report its visions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel recounts that solitary study is often ruined by surrounding animal and environmental noises (a long catalogue of bird, beast, and domestic sounds) and compares the effect of hunger and bodily disturbance on dreaming. The body must be at ease so the 'animal spirits' can function and convey images to the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gates of Sleep: horn vs ivory distinction for dream veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams that come through the gate of horn are true and certain; dreams through the gate of ivory are confused, doubtful, and false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor explained: horn (diaphanous, transparent) lets clear images pass and produce true dreams; ivory (opaque) yields confused, uncertain dreams. The distinction is used to evaluate whether a dream should be trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of petty superstitious amulets and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel warns against reliance on charms and curious items (laurel under pillow, crocodile shoulder, Bactrian stones, Ammonian horn) as guarantees of true dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices are called superstitious and their 'cheat' is exposed by authorities (Serapion Ascalonites, Antiphon, Philochorus, Artemon, Fulgentius Planciades). The narrator treats these as unreliable and unnecessary for genuine divination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation over extreme fasting or abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: While some authorities prescribe extreme fasts to induce or improve dreams, Pantagruel counsels moderation: neither gluttony nor excessive fasting aids prophetic insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel criticizes hermits' long fasts as producing 'saltless, dry, jejune' writings and argues that completely empty bodies make spirits languid; recommends a modest light supper and warns against rigorous abstinence as counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: No appeal from the decrees of Fortune (legal-philosophical point)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text relays the legal/philosophical principle that one cannot appeal from the decrees of Fortune: Fortune acknowledges no superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Baldus (Lib. ult. Cap. de Leg.) is invoked to argue that there is no appellate remedy against the sentence of fate or lot—used to rebut an appeal against an unfavorable lot-reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common symbolic motifs and their contested interpretations (horns, beating, theft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain images/verses have conventional symbolic readings (e.g., horns = cuckoldry or horn of plenty/abundance; being beaten = marital chastisement; theft = spouse will steal from husband), but interpretations vary and may be inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Panurge vs Pantagruel: the same verse(s) are read differently—Panurge insists horns mean abundance (cornucopia), Pantagruel and others insist they mean cuckoldry. Text references Artemidorus and other dream commentators and shows interpretive disagreement; readers are warned that symbolism is contestable.
